problems.title: String identity does not establish semantic equivalence
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, PDF p.5; Appendix B.5, PDF p.18, Table 8
claim: Section 3.3 compares generated formula strings with source formulas and then describes the natural-language reasoning as validated.
analysis: The valid symbolic tree is \(P\to Q,P\vdash Q\). Let the English first premise instead mean \(Q\to P\), while attaching the expected string \(P\to Q\). Every formula-string comparison passes. The valuation \(P=\mathrm{true},Q=\mathrm{false}\) satisfies the actual English premises and falsifies the conclusion. This is a constructed failure of certification, not an observed training row. Appendix B.5 separately reports consistency judgments of \(97.6\%\) and \(96.8\%\).
result: The gate does not supply a universal semantic-validity guarantee. The source already presents quality improvement and residual fallibility.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.
repair: A sound symbolic tree yields a valid English conclusion if every instantiated statement is semantically equivalent to its formula. String matching does not prove that additional premise; no corrected dataset is established.
problems.impact_rationale: This is an overstrong validation interpretation, with no demonstrated large error in the actual generated collection.
problems.existing_correction_status: An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.
